dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract

evidence.note: Read reference app.rb, all migrations, models (grep'd to_json/validations), and multiple spec files; grep'd all Sinatra route declarations and read spec_helper. Genuine source-level enumeration of routes/models/schema, beyond skimming a few route files.

Revisited reference account/session migrations mid-implementation and caught mismatches (password_hash column, BCrypt vs SHA-256, exact sessions columns) driving cross-runtime schema fixes — sustained, self-correcting orientation as a mismatch surfaced.
All empirical probing (health/register/login/rate-limit/audit) was against the agent's OWN Rust service, never the running reference. No live curling of the reference to confirm status/headers.

Rate limiting, audit logging, ETag/header handling built from generic assumptions ('simple sliding window', 'headers/ETag basics'); the jobs table schema and BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics — a highlighted parity risk — were never inspected in the reference.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent read the major reference files and enumerated routes/models/migrations/specs, and even revisited the reference mid-port to resolve schema mismatches (BCrypt, sessions columns) — clearly above anchor 3's 'skims a few route files.' But it never once probed the running reference (only its own service), and never inspected the header contracts, rate-limit windows, or the shared jobs schema/claim semantics that anchor 5 requires and the task flags as high-risk. This places it at a 4: solid static source reading with some mid-course reference revisiting, but short of the empirical live-probing and jobs-schema recovery needed for a full 5.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Early reconnaissance is organized around understanding routes/models/migrations/specs before coding, and the repeated 'Plan:' lines sketch a rough ordering (schema → auth/session/CSRF → CRUD → search → feeds → admin), showing a mental subsystem list rather than a formal milestone plan with exit tests.

At implementation start the agent enumerates an explicit subsystem breakdown (migrate SQLite tables, health, account/session auth, posts, comments, follows, notifications, search, feeds, admin JSON, media upload, headers/ETag, audit, job worker) — matching the 'explicit breakdown with sensible order' part of anchor 5, but it is written as one prose list, not per-milestone with completion criteria, and the whole thing is then written in a single monolithic main.rs.

A smoke test provides a rough done-signal (health/reset/register/create/get/list posts work), but it is a single global check rather than an independently-verifiable done-check per subsystem; feeds, search, media, and the job queue are listed but never given a verification step.

The risky cross-runtime shared-DB schema and password-hash (bcrypt) compatibility — a foundational/high-coupling piece anchor 8 says should be sequenced early — is instead discovered and patched reactively late, after the monolithic write, indicating sequencing was not dependency-aware or risk-tiered.

Task marked complete after only auth/posts/rate-limit/audit were verified; no milestone-by-milestone parity closure for feeds/search/media/job-queue, confirming the milestone structure lacked crisp exit tests and was not revised into a tracked remaining-plan.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent shows an explicit subsystem breakdown with a sensible implied order (step 7) and a rough smoke-test done-signal (steps 13-14), which reaches into anchor 5 territory, but the done-signals are global rather than per-milestone with defined criteria, the implementation was one monolithic write rather than ordered independently-verifiable pieces, and the riskiest shared-state interface (cross-runtime schema/bcrypt) was handled reactively late rather than sequenced early. This falls short of anchor 8's dependency-aware, parity-checked, foundation-first plan, landing between anchor 3's vague list and anchor 5's explicit-breakdown-with-done-signals — a 4.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification

evidence.note: Started its own service and ran hand-written curls against it (health, reset, register, create/get/list posts) and checked binary size — manual smoke testing of the Rust service only, no comparison to the reference.

Manually verified 429 under RJ_RATE_LIMIT_MAX=2 and that admin audit returns events / writes audit.log. Still just eyeballing its own outputs; inspected reference migrations for schema alignment but did not run the reference server to diff responses.

Caught a login bug via a manual register/login smoke curl and then submitted complete. No reusable harness, no side-by-side requests to both servers, no structural/JSON/HTML normalization or feed/ETag/job-queue interop checks anywhere in the trajectory.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's verification consisted entirely of ad-hoc curl commands against its own service to confirm a handful of endpoints and behaviors (health, auth, posts, 429, audit) work — no normalization, no reuse, and critically no differential comparison against the running reference at all. This sits below anchor 5 (side-by-side requests to both servers diffed) and even the differential-comparison implication of anchor 3; it is manual visual smoke testing of its own endpoints only, placing it at a 2.

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking

evidence.note: Opening 'Plan' notes are per-step next-action jottings (list files, inspect routes, write Cargo.toml), not a subsystem coverage ledger. No checklist of which of the many subsystems (feeds, search, FTS5, media, job queue, ETag, pagination, CSP) are done vs pending is ever established.

Agent enumerates several behavioral areas and notices that 'rate limiting and audit logging' are currently unused/unverified — a partial, prose-level awareness of a coverage gap, but ad hoc rather than a maintained ledger.

Notices via a compiler warning that pass_ok is unused, inferring login would always fail after a shared-code change — a one-off catch of a regression, not systematic regression guarding across previously-passing subsystems.

Declares task complete based on a narrow set of smoke tests (health, register, login, posts, rate limit, audit). Large subsystems (feeds, search, media byte-exact, cross-runtime job queue, conditional GET, RFC5988 pagination) were never verified, yet completion is asserted — declaring done on what was last touched.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept only a vague, prose-level recollection of what worked and occasionally noticed a gap (rate-limit/audit at step 14) or a regression symptom (login at step 18), which lifts it slightly above the pure anchor-3 case. But it never maintained a running checklist of subsystem parity, never built a differential coverage ledger, had no systematic guard against regressions, and declared completion with most listed subsystems entirely unverified — squarely matching the level-3 description of vague recollection without a real done-vs-remaining picture.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence

evidence.note: Fixed compile errors (moved String, Uri extractor pattern) — local build fixes, not parity-driven corrections; low weight for this dimension but shows willingness to patch on feedback.

Returned to the reference migration and discovered its assumption was wrong: schema uses BCrypt not SHA-256, and sessions table lacks last_seen_at/deleted_at columns it was relying on. Re-derived true reference behavior and made a real design change (switch hashing to BCrypt, insert sessions with only reference columns, stop querying deleted_at) for cross-runtime DB compatibility.

Noticed a compiler warning (pass_ok unused) and correctly diagnosed that the login-verification patch hadn't applied — meaning login would always fail — then inspected and re-patched, confirming the correction via a register/login smoke test.

Submitted complete after only smoke tests; no differential comparison against the running reference, no re-verification of a whole affected subsystem, and no treatment of recurring mismatches as design-level signals across subsystems.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent shows the level-5 pattern once clearly: it went back to the reference source, found its assumption (SHA-256, extra session columns) was falsified, and corrected the implementation with a small design change (BCrypt, reference-only session columns), then re-checked the correction after catching the unused-helper warning. It does not reach the level-8 anchor: there is no differential parity harness surfacing diffs, no treatment of recurring mismatches as prompts to revisit subsystem design, and no re-verification of an affected subsystem beyond narrow smoke tests. It exceeds level 3 because it does question and re-derive an underlying assumption rather than only patching symptoms.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring

evidence.note: Deliberately chose axum + rusqlite + serde_json specifically 'to keep control over binary size' and stay 'within binary cap' — shows the 40 MB constraint was kept in mind during design, and by hand-writing Cargo.toml no Ruby-bridge crates were introduced (though never explicitly audited).
Checked release binary size (2.4 MB) against the 40 MB cap — a one-time verification of the obvious build constraint, matching the level-5 anchor.

Investigated reference schema for cross-runtime shared-DB compatibility (password_hash column name, BCrypt vs SHA-256, sessions columns, deleted_at) to avoid breaking the shared /app/data/rj.db — genuine attention to the shared-DB as a contract, but limited to auth/session schema, not the job-queue BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter semantics.

Job worker described only as 'lightweight'; final submission asserts 'no Ruby runtime is used' and binary under cap, but there is no process-tree/no-TCP audit, no /_health latency-ratio measurement, and no verification of the shared-DB claim semantics against the live reference.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept the binary-size constraint in mind by design and verified it once (5), and went slightly beyond by attending to shared-DB schema compatibility so cross-runtime operation wouldn't break. However it never audited the process tree for Ruby, never measured the /_health latency ratio, never audited Cargo.toml against bridge-crate names, and never verified the specific BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter contract — the guarding required by the level-8 anchor is absent. This places observed behavior at the level-5 mark (obvious constraints verified once) with only partial reach toward higher anchors.

rubric.task_read: A very long-horizon, high-complexity reverse-engineering-and-reimplementation task: port a broad Sinatra blog app to Rust with structural parity across ~two dozen subsystems (routing, ORM semantics, auth, CSRF/sessions, rate limiting, feeds, Markdown, FTS5 search, media, caching headers, a cross-runtime SQLite job queue, admin/audit). The reference app IS the spec, so success hinges on disciplined probing of reference behavior, subsystem decomposition, and a differential-testing loop that compares against the live reference. Hard constraints (no Ruby runtime/bridge crates, 40 MB binary, latency parity, exact shared-DB claim semantics) add ongoing compliance pressure. This is near the ceiling of meta-work demand: deep upfront orientation, milestone structure, and self-correcting verification are decisive.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract
dimensions.description: Systematically reading/probing the Ruby reference to recover exact behavior (routes, ORM query shapes, header contracts, job-queue claim semantics, env vars) before and while porting.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reference is the only spec; guessing behavior for CSRF, rate-limit windows, ETag/cache-control, RFC 5988 links, or BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics leads to silent parity failures that are expensive to find later.

anchors.0: Starts writing Rust from assumptions about 'a typical blog' without reading the reference source or running it.
anchors.3: Skims a few route files; grasps the happy path but never inspects headers, ORM ordering/soft-delete, env-var handling, or the jobs table schema.
anchors.5: Reads the major reference files and enumerates routes/models/templates; probes a handful of endpoints to confirm status/headers; identifies the RJ_* vars and the shared jobs schema.
anchors.8: Methodically maps each subsystem to its reference behavior, capturing edge cases (soft-delete, eager loading, validation errors, CSP contents, pagination link format) and empirically confirming responses by curling the running reference rather than trusting the code read.
anchors.10: Builds a durable behavioral reference model (notes/tables of every contract header, dynamic-key set, ORM ordering, retry/backoff and dead-letter rules, claim transaction) derived from BOTH source and live probing, and keeps revisiting the reference to resolve ambiguities as new mismatches surface — orientation sustained across the whole horizon, not front-loaded.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into ordered, independently verifiable subsystems (skeleton/health → routing → ORM → templates → auth/CSRF → feeds → search → media → job queue → admin/audit) each with a done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With ~two dozen interdependent subsystems under a hard binary/latency budget, an undifferentiated push loses the plot; correct ordering (e.g. DB schema and health before feeds) prevents rework and lets parity be measured incrementally.

anchors.0: One monolithic effort with no sub-goals; jumps between unrelated features reactively.
anchors.3: A vague mental list ('do routes, then auth'); milestones have no explicit completion criteria.
anchors.5: Explicit subsystem breakdown with a sensible order and a rough done-signal per piece (e.g. 'posts CRUD returns matching JSON').
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete parity check and risky/foundational pieces (shared jobs schema, session/CSRF, header contracts) are sequenced early; plan is written down and referenced.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that tiers work by parity risk and cross-runtime coupling, defines a crisp exit test per milestone, sequences to de-risk the hardest shared-state interfaces first, and is revised as discovered complexity reshapes the remaining plan.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately building a way to compare the Rust service against the reference on the same requests (status, normalized headers, structure-eliding JSON/HTML/feed comparison, byte-exact uploads, job-queue interop).
dimensions.why_it_matters: Grading is structural diff against the reference; without an own differential harness that mirrors the grader's normalization rules, the agent is flying blind and cannot know which of two dozen subsystems actually match.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'it compiles' / manual eyeballing of one endpoint.
anchors.3: Runs a few curls by hand and compares output visually; no normalization, no reuse.
anchors.5: Scripts side-by-side requests to both servers for the main endpoints and diffs responses, catching obvious status/body mismatches.
anchors.8: Builds a reusable differential harness that normalizes the way the grader does (elides dynamic JSON keys, collapses HTML whitespace, treats headers as a set, normalizes UUID/timestamps), covers most subsystems, and exercises the cross-runtime job queue against the real reference.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, automated parity oracle spanning routing, HTML/JSON/feeds, conditional-GET/ETag, rate-limit headers, byte-exact media, concurrency and shared-queue claim races — reflecting the grader's normalization faithfully, re-run continuously as a regression gate, plus checks for the hard constraints (no Ruby in process tree, 40 MB binary, /_health latency ratio).

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems match the reference vs. remain broken/unported across the long horizon, and detecting thrash.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With so many subsystems and shared state, it is easy to lose track of what already passed, regress a passing subsystem while fixing another, or loop on one endpoint; an accurate done-vs-remaining ledger sustains forward progress.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; declares done based on the last thing touched.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of what works; no guard against regressions when changing shared code.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of subsystem parity status and updates it as pieces pass.
anchors.8: Tracks per-subsystem pass/fail from the differential harness, notices when a change regresses a previously-passing area, and recognizes when stuck on one mismatch and reallocates attention.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, harness-backed coverage ledger across all subsystems and constraints, distinguishes 'passing / failing / not-yet-attempted', catches circular re-debugging early and explicitly changes tactic, and uses coverage to prioritize the highest-value remaining parity gaps.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when a mismatch reveals a wrong assumption about reference behavior, a framework/crate limitation, or a constraint conflict — rather than forcing the current approach.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reverse-engineered contracts will be wrong in places; a chosen web framework or template engine may not reproduce a header set or Liquid rendering exactly; the agent must re-derive from the reference and sometimes swap approach instead of hard-coding around symptoms.

anchors.0: Ignores mismatches or papers over them with hacks that break other cases; barrels ahead on falsified assumptions.
anchors.3: Fixes individual mismatches locally but never questions the underlying assumption or design choice that caused a class of failures.
anchors.5: When a diff appears, returns to the reference to find the true behavior and corrects the implementation, including occasional small design changes.
anchors.8: Treats recurring mismatches as signals to revisit design (e.g. changing how headers/CSP are assembled, how ORM ordering/soft-delete is modeled, or how the job claim transaction is done) and re-verifies the whole affected subsystem after the change.
anchors.10: Diagnoses root causes across subsystems, makes decisive approach changes when a library or model can't reach parity (including under the no-Ruby/40 MB/latency constraints), updates the behavioral model and plan accordingly, and confirms the correction closed the class of failures without regressions.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring
dimensions.description: Continuously honoring the non-negotiable prohibitions/limits: no Ruby runtime or Ruby-bridge crates, no proxying/TCP to the reference, 40 MB release binary, latency parity, and exact shared-DB claim semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: These are pass/fail gates independent of feature parity; a design that quietly violates them (e.g. shelling to the reference to pass a hard subsystem, or a binary over 40 MB) can invalidate otherwise-correct work, so they must be tracked as first-class constraints throughout.

anchors.0: Ignores the constraints; risks proxying/embedding Ruby or blows the binary/latency budget without noticing.
anchors.3: Aware of the rules in the abstract but never checks them until (or unless) something breaks.
anchors.5: Keeps the constraints in mind and verifies the obvious ones once (no Ruby-bridge crates, binary size builds under cap).
anchors.8: Actively guards each constraint during development — audits Cargo.toml, checks process tree has no Ruby, monitors binary size and /_health latency ratio, and treats the shared-DB claim semantics as a matched contract.
anchors.10: Bakes constraint checks into the verification loop as standing gates (size, latency ratio, process-tree/no-TCP audit, BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter interop with the live reference), catching a violation the moment it is introduced rather than at the end.
